subject: psych
title: Kitty Genovese (1964): thirty-eight witnesses, and the story psychology told
dek: A Kew Gardens murder, a New York Times parable, the bystander effect — and the later correction that fewer people saw, and some people acted.
text: Kitty Genovese (1964): thirty-eight witnesses, and the story psychology told A Kew Gardens murder, a New York Times parable, the bystander effect — and the later correction that fewer people saw, and some people acted. 1964, and after Kitty Genovese was a person, not a teaching aid. This capsule does not describe wounds and does not use a corpse as a figure. The New York Times story of “38 witnesses” is treated as a historical object that psychology used — and that later historians and psychologists, especially Manning, Levine, and Collins (American Psychologist, 2007), showed was not supported by the record. The bystander-effect experiments are a separate object from the parable. Psych / soc psych 13 Mar 1964 Kew Gardens Genovese is attacked near her home after work. She dies. A neighbor, Sophia Farrar, goes to her. 27 Mar 1964 The Times Martin Gansberg’s New York Times story: 37 (later 38) who saw and did not call. The parable is set. 1968–70 The lab Latané and Darley publish the bystander studies the parable helped to authorize. 2007 The correction Manning, Levine, and Collins: no good evidence for 38 watchers, or for total inaction. 2014–16 The books A second public correction, including Kevin Cook’s Kitty Genovese. Textbooks begin, unevenly, to catch up. now The double lesson What groups do to helping — and what a discipline does when it falls in love with a story. The Times story is two weeks later, not the next morning Genovese was killed on 13 March 1964. Gansberg’s New York Times article ran on 27 March. The parable was not a live dispatch from the sidewalk. It was a constructed account, two weeks on, that already knew what it wanted the city to mean. That gap is part of how a crime became a syllabus. bystander effect bystander intervention Genovese syndrome The well-replicated finding that people are often less likely to help in an emergency when others are present. Latané and Darley’s experiments are the core. “Genovese syndrome” is a later popular name. The effect does not depend on the 38-witnesses story being true. diffusion of responsibility One mechanism in the bystander research: if others can help, each person feels less personally required to. A lab result, not a moral insult to a whole neighborhood. pluralistic ignorance Another mechanism: if nobody else looks alarmed, people read the situation as not an emergency. Calm faces become false information. 38 witnesses thirty-eight witnesses 37 who saw The New York Times’s number. Gansberg’s 27 March 1964 story used 37; 38 became the frozen figure. Manning, Levine, and Collins (2007) argue the archive does not support 38 people watching a murder and doing nothing. Kew Gardens A neighborhood in Queens, New York, around the LIRR station and Austin Street. Genovese lived near the station and was attacked in that small geography — street, lot, a building entry — not on a stage in front of a stadium. Martin Gansberg New York Times reporter. His 27 March 1964 article, with editor A. M. Rosenthal’s interest, made the 38-witnesses story national. The piece is a primary object. It is not a trial transcript. Bibb Latané Latané Social psychologist. With John Darley, ran the 1960s experiments that became the bystander-effect literature. The studies are real. The newspaper parable is the thing they and textbooks often used as a hook. John Darley Darley Social psychologist, Princeton and elsewhere. Co-author of the early bystander papers. The lab is his and Latané’s; the Times story is not. Sophia Farrar A neighbor who went to Genovese, held her, and stayed until help came. Her name is part of the correction: “nobody helped” is false. Manning, Levine and Collins Manning Levine Collins Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins. Their 2007 American Psychologist article, “The parable of the 38 witnesses,” is the academic correction this capsule follows. parable A story told for a moral, not because every detail survived checking. Manning et al. use the word on purpose: psychology needed a story about the danger of the group, and the Times had supplied one. Austin Street The Kew Gardens street along the LIRR. The attacks happened in this small outdoor and entry geography, not in a single apartment window’s full view for half an hour — which is one reason the “38 watched the whole thing” sentence fails. Before A neighborhood, a station, a night shift Kew Gardens in 1964 was a Queens neighborhood organized around a Long Island Rail Road station, a few bars and shops, and apartment houses that looked at one another across a small street. Catherine “Kitty” Genovese, 28, managed a bar. She was driving home in the early hours of 13 March when she was attacked near the station. She was a person going home. That is the whole of the “before” this capsule needs. Kew Gardens, west to east, about 1936 — a generation before 1964. The neighborhood was already a grid of houses and apartment blocks around the railroad. The crime did not invent the place. The parable later made the place a stage. Wide panoramic photograph of Kew Gardens, Long Island, looking west to east, about 1936. Lefferts Boulevard and the station, 2019. Genovese’s last walk was a short geography: car, street, a building entry. The modern shops are not 1964. The crossing still is. Lefferts Boulevard view toward the Kew Gardens LIRR station and neighborhood shops. The era A crime, a newspaper, a laboratory Winston Moseley attacked Genovese, left, and came back. She died. A neighbor, Sophia Farrar, went to her. Other neighbors heard something; some looked; at least one account has a man shouting from a window; some contact with the police happened, in ways the later parable flattened. The trial established a killer. It did not establish a stadium of watchers. The walkway from the Kew Gardens station toward Lefferts Boulevard, 2019 — a place later labeled as part of the crime’s geography. It is an alley in daylight. This capsule will not reconstruct the night on top of it. A paved alley and walkway near the Kew Gardens LIRR station, photographed in 2019. On 27 March 1964 the New York Times published Martin Gansberg’s story, headed as 37 who saw a murder and did not call the police. Thirty-eight became the number that stuck. A. M. Rosenthal, at the Times, made the story a civic diagnosis: the city had gone cold. That diagnosis is a 1964 New York object — crime, race, a newspaper’s voice — as much as it is a fact about one street. Social psychology took the story as a gift. Bibb Latané and John Darley designed experiments in which smoke filled a room, or a cry for help came from another room, and the variable was whether other people were present. People helped less when they were not alone. Diffusion of responsibility; pluralistic ignorance. Those studies replicated. They are the science. The 38 witnesses are the hook the science used in its textbooks. Windows facing a station and a lot. The Times story asked readers to imagine dozens of people at those windows for the length of a murder. The later correction is partly architectural: who could see what, from where, for how long. Kew Gardens station and the Mowbray apartments from Lefferts Boulevard. The same years, elsewhere: 1964 is also Freedom Summer, the Civil Rights Act, Tokyo’s Olympics, the Gulf of Tonkin. Kew Gardens is not the world’s only street. This capsule stays on this street because the case is about how a local crime became a universal lesson — and what got trimmed to make the lesson travel. A mid-century New York crowd — Times Square, not Kew Gardens, and earlier than 1964. It is here as the city the Times was writing about: density, strangers, a public that can be narrated as cold. Kew Gardens was quieter than this. The parable borrowed the city’s scale anyway. Crowded New York street with a City Omnibus bus, Walgreens, and sailors, mid-century. People The woman, the neighbor, the reporters, the lab Catherine “Kitty” Genovese 1935–1964 Born in Brooklyn, lived in Kew Gardens, managed a bar. The capsule uses her name and her dates. It does not use her body as a figure. The 1961 police photograph that circulates online is a booking photo from another year. It is not used here. Sophia Farrar neighbor Went to Genovese, held her, waited for help. If the parable needs a moral, start with the person who crossed the street — and with the fact that the parable left her out. Martin Gansberg / A. M. Rosenthal The Times, 1964 The reporter and the editor who made 37/38 a national sentence. Journalism is an actor in this case, not a window. Latané and Darley 1960s–70s papers The experimenters. Their results about groups and helping do not become false if the newspaper story shrinks. That is the distinction this capsule exists to keep. A story The parable of the 38 In 2007, in American Psychologist, Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins went back to the archive. They argued there is no good evidence that 38 people witnessed the murder, that they watched it through, or that they all remained inactive. Some people could not see. Some heard and did not understand. Some did act. The Times story had become, in their word, a parable: a tale about the danger of the group that textbooks needed, and that then limited what the field asked next — for example, how a group can also make helping more likely. A discipline can be right about a mechanism and wrong about a corpse. Both parts of that sentence have to stay. After Textbooks, and a slower correction The bystander effect remained one of social psychology’s most taught results. The 38-witnesses story remained, for a long time, the first paragraph. Later textbooks began to qualify it; some did not. A 2015 study of intro texts found the old story still in circulation. Correction in a science is not only a 2007 paper. It is whether the next edition deletes a sentence. The case now teaches two things, if it is taught honestly: how the presence of others can inhibit help — and how a field tells itself origin stories. Kitty Genovese is not improved by being useful. She is owed a street that is not only a graph. A question Leave this on the table When a science needs a parable, whose life gets simplified to make the moral travel? Manning, Levine & Collins (2007) — American Psychologist The correction, as a paper. Abstract on PubMed; the PDF is behind a publisher wall. Not a true-crime film.

subject: business
title: Cursor (2022–26): why an AI editor broke out
dek: Anysphere’s bet: put the model in the editor, not beside it — and compete with Copilot on that ground.
text: Cursor (2022–26): why an AI editor broke out Anysphere’s bet: put the model in the editor, not beside it — and compete with Copilot on that ground. 2022–2026 This is a strategy case, not a profile of genius. Numbers appear only when a named public source states them. TechCrunch (11 October 2023; 5 June 2025) and GitHub’s own Copilot announcement (29 June 2021) are the spine. Cursor’s public site, including a 14 August 2026 company post titled as the firm now being part of SpaceX, is cited as the company’s own speech — not as independently audited finance. Revenue, valuation, and headcount that lack a named source are omitted. No invented slogans. No fake founder portraits. Business business 2021 Copilot GitHub and OpenAI announce Copilot, 29 June 2021: autocomplete inside the editor you already have. 2022 Anysphere Four MIT classmates incorporate. The product will be a fork, not a plugin. 2023 Seed TechCrunch, 11 October: $8 million seed led by the OpenAI Startup Fund; total raised $11 million. 2024–25 Category A crowd of AI editors and agents. Copilot is the incumbent. Others try the same door. 2025 Series C TechCrunch, 5 June 2025: $900 million at a $9.9 billion valuation, citing Bloomberg; Thrive Capital leads. 2026 Company post Cursor’s site lists a 14 August 2026 post: the company is now part of SpaceX. This capsule does not add a price. They told TechCrunch they would not clone and sell In the 11 October 2023 TechCrunch interview, CEO Michael Truell said the “ceiling in the AI coding space is so high” that it was “not possible to just clone the tech and then put great sales on top.” Whether that remains a good description of the category is a 2026 question. The quote is useful because it is dated and attributed: a five-person company, just seeded, explaining why it thought Microsoft’s distribution advantage was not the whole game. Cursor AI-centered code editor made by Anysphere. TechCrunch (2023) described it as a fork of Microsoft’s VS Code: the familiar editor, rebuilt so generation, chat, and codebase questions live inside it. Anysphere The company that makes Cursor. Incorporated 2022. TechCrunch names the founders as Michael Truell, Sualeh Asif, Arvid Lunnemark, and Aman Sanger, who met at MIT. VS Code Visual Studio Code Microsoft’s free, widely used code editor. Stack Overflow’s 2023 survey, cited in TechCrunch’s seed story, put it far ahead of other editors. Cursor’s bet was to fork it rather than live as a plugin inside it. fork A copy of a software project that goes its own way. Cursor forked VS Code so Anysphere could change the editor itself — not only add a sidebar — while keeping the keybindings and extensions people already knew. GitHub Copilot Copilot GitHub and OpenAI’s AI pair-programmer, announced 29 June 2021. It began as completions inside VS Code and other editors: the incumbent Cursor had to differentiate from. IDE integrated development environment A program that gathers editing, running, debugging, and project tools in one place. Anysphere’s 2023 pitch, per TechCrunch, was an “AI-native” IDE — the model as a default, not an add-on. ARR annual recurring revenue Subscription revenue expressed as a yearly run rate. TechCrunch’s 2023 seed story said Anysphere claimed ARR already over $1 million. The 2025 story reports later ARR figures via Bloomberg and sources. This capsule does not invent a current number. OpenAI Startup Fund OpenAI’s early-stage fund. TechCrunch, 11 October 2023: it led Cursor’s $8 million seed, with angels including former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman and Dropbox co-founder Arash Ferdowsi. Thrive Capital Venture firm. TechCrunch, 5 June 2025: it led a $900 million round valuing Anysphere at $9.9 billion, with a16z, Accel, and DST also named. agent coding agent cloud agent In this product category, software that can take a multi-step programming task — edit files, run commands, sometimes open a browser — rather than only complete the current line. Cursor’s public site in 2026 sells agents as the center. The word is the company’s; the capability is what to test. tab completion autocomplete Suggesting the next tokens as you type. Copilot made this the default picture of “AI plus coding.” Anysphere’s 2023 comment to TechCrunch, via co-founder Aman Sanger, was that they wanted the features after autocomplete: bugs, codebase Q&A, edits across files. Windsurf Another AI coding assistant. TechCrunch’s 5 June 2025 piece notes OpenAI’s reported purchase of Windsurf after Anysphere, the same story says, turned down acquisition approaches. A competitor, named because a named source named it. Before The plugin and the editor you already had On 29 June 2021 GitHub announced Copilot: an “AI pair programmer” that suggested lines and functions inside Visual Studio Code. The model (OpenAI Codex, in that announcement) lived where the programmer already was. That is the incumbent move. You do not switch editors. You install a habit. GitHub’s own 2021 launch art: “Your AI pair programmer,” a completion highlighted in the editor. This is the product Cursor had to be other than — not a distant cousin, a sitting tenant. GitHub Copilot 2021 announcement graphic: Your AI pair programmer, with a code-completion example. By 2023, per TechCrunch’s seed story, VS Code was the default editor for a large majority of developers in Stack Overflow’s survey that year. A new IDE that ignored that fact was a hobby. A new IDE that was a fork of that fact was a strategy. Microsoft’s public VS Code art, later in the same category: the incumbent editor selling AI as a redefinition of itself. Cursor’s 2023 bet was to fork this editor rather than live only as a guest inside it. Visual Studio Code marketing graphic: Your code editor. Redefined with AI. The era Fork the editor, then sell the difference Anysphere incorporated in 2022. The four founders — Michael Truell, Sualeh Asif, Arvid Lunnemark, Aman Sanger — had met at MIT. TechCrunch’s 11 October 2023 piece is the public origin story this capsule will use: an $8 million seed led by the OpenAI Startup Fund, total raised $11 million, a five-person company, ARR “already over $1 million” as Truell claimed to the reporter. Those are the numbers a named source printed. Later headlines are later headlines. The mark as Cursor’s public site served it: a cube, an arrow, a name. A wordmark is not a valuation. It is what a product uses when it wants to be recognized in a tab. CURSOR wordmark and cube mark on black, from the company’s public Open Graph image. The product difference, in that 2023 interview, is not “we also complete code.” Sanger said Copilot and others had done autocomplete “particularly well,” and that Cursor was aimed at what comes after: questions about a codebase, finding bugs, edits that are not the next token. The company forked VS Code so those features could be native — keybindings familiar, extensions familiar, the AI not a guest. From the public homepage: the editor as a place where generation, errors, and a repo can share one glass. Whether this is “after autocomplete” is a user’s judgment. The screenshot is the pitch. Dark editor, terminal, and repository windows on a monitor, from Cursor’s homepage. The same years, not as decoration: Copilot kept shipping; other tools (TechCrunch’s 2025 piece names Windsurf in the context of an OpenAI acquisition) tried the same category; models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and others became interchangeable parts. Cursor’s site, by 2026, sells “agents” that can take a task for minutes or hours. That is a later product sentence. The 2023 sentence was: own the editor. A still from Cursor’s public homepage: a working session, “Background agent” on the board. This capsule does not name the speaker. The board is the product language the company chose to show. A man gesturing in front of a blackboard that says Background agent and Set up environment, from Cursor’s homepage. On 5 June 2025 TechCrunch reported a $900 million round at a $9.9 billion valuation, led by Thrive Capital, and said Bloomberg had the company past $500 million ARR. Those figures are attributed in that article. They are not re-audited here. On 14 August 2026 Cursor’s own site listed a company post: Cursor is now part of SpaceX. This capsule records the company’s statement. It does not invent a price, a share count, or a culture memo to go with it. People A company, an incumbent, a fund Michael Truell CEO, Anysphere Named by TechCrunch (2023) as co-founder and CEO. The quotes this capsule uses — mission, Microsoft as competitor, the “ceiling” in AI coding — are from that interview. No biography beyond the source. Aman Sanger Co-founder Named in the same 2023 piece. The useful sentence is his: autocomplete was already done well; they wanted the work after it. A product position, attributed. GitHub Copilot Announced 2021 Not a person. The sitting product. Cursor’s case only makes sense if Copilot is in the room: distribution, Microsoft, the habit of completing the next line. The incumbent’s own art. A story Distribution versus the native editor TechCrunch asked, in 2023, whether a five-person fork could compete with Microsoft. Truell’s answer was that VS Code’s breadth was also a brake: Microsoft could not change the editor radically without risking the people who already lived there. Cursor, being small and specialized, could. That is a classic disruptor paragraph. It may or may not remain true once a product is no longer small. The case is useful because the paragraph is dated. You can watch what happened after. The strategic object is not a model. Models are rented. The object is the place the programmer’s hands already are, and whether “AI” is a guest in that place or the room itself. After A category, then a parent company By 2025–26 the category had a name in the press — sometimes “vibe coding,” sometimes “coding agents” — and more than one well-funded tool. Copilot did not leave. Cursor’s public site, in August 2026, presented agents, cloud machines, and a company post about SpaceX. A later Saturday capsule can take the acquisition as a case of its own, with filings. This one stops at what a named article and the company’s own page have already said. The lesson for a strategy notebook is older than any of these names: if the incumbent owns the habit (the editor), you either live as a plugin inside the habit or you try to own a new habit that feels like the old one. Cursor chose the second. The bill for that choice is not printed here. A question Leave this on the table If the model is rented, what, exactly, did the editor company sell? Introducing GitHub Copilot (29 June 2021) GitHub’s own announcement. The incumbent’s product page, not a recap. Anysphere raises $8M — TechCrunch, 11 October 2023 Named source for the seed, the fork-of-VS-Code description, and the founders’ names. Cursor’s Anysphere nabs $9.9B valuation — TechCrunch, 5 June 2025 Named source for the 2025 round. ARR figures in that piece are attributed to Bloomberg and to sources. Cursor — product site The company’s current public pitch, including the 14 August 2026 company post listed on the homepage.

subject: history
title: War of Resistance (1937–45): the war that did not wait for 1939
dek: From the Marco Polo Bridge to Chongqing — a world war looked at from China, not as Asia’s footnote to Europe.
text: War of Resistance (1937–45): the war that did not wait for 1939 From the Marco Polo Bridge to Chongqing — a world war looked at from China, not as Asia’s footnote to Europe. 1937–1945 This capsule looks out from China. Europe’s 1939 is contemporaneous, not the frame. “World War II” as a 1939–45 European story leaves 1937–39 as a preface. From Chongqing, 1939 is the year the European war caught up. Nanjing is treated with one careful image of a city after bombing — no corpses as illustration. Casualty figures that cannot be sourced here are omitted. History history 1931–32 Mukden / Lytton Japan seizes Manchuria. The League’s Lytton Commission investigates. The full-scale war is still ahead. 1937 Lugou / Shanghai 7 July at the Marco Polo Bridge; the Battle of Shanghai from August. 1937 Nanjing The capital falls in December. Massacre follows. This capsule will not decorate that fact. 1938–43 Chongqing Wartime capital. Years of bombing. A city that had to go underground. 1939 Europe Germany invades Poland. A second opening, not the first. 1945 Surrender / after Japan surrenders. The civil war does not wait long. Memory becomes a second fight. Europeans named the bridge for a traveler The stone bridge at Wanping is 盧溝橋, the Lugou Bridge. Europeans called it the Marco Polo Bridge because Polo’s Travels describe a fine bridge in this region. The 1937 incident entered English under the traveler’s name. The soldiers at Wanping were not fighting over a memoir. They were fighting over a crossing and a railway town. The nickname is a European filing label that stuck. War of Resistance 抗日戰爭 Second Sino-Japanese War Chinese name for the full-scale war with Japan, conventionally dated from 7 July 1937 to 1945. Some Chinese histories include 1931. This capsule uses 1937–45 as the full-scale span and treats 1931 as the before. Marco Polo Bridge Lugou Bridge 盧溝橋 Lugouqiao Stone bridge over the Yongding River near Wanping, southwest of Beiping. A clash beginning 7 July 1937 became the opening of full-scale war. Europeans had long called it the Marco Polo Bridge. Wanping 宛平 Walled town at the north end of the Lugou Bridge. The 1937 incident is a fight over a railway town and a crossing, not a metaphor. United Front Second United Front The uneasy wartime cooperation between the Nationalists (KMT) and the Communists after 1937, following the Xi’an Incident of 1936. A front is not a friendship. It is an agreement about who the enemy is this year. Chongqing Chungking 重慶 Sichuan city that became the Nationalist wartime capital after the fall of Nanjing and the retreat up the Yangtze. Japanese bombing of the city, 1938–43, is one of the long air campaigns of the war. Battle of Shanghai August–November 1937. Urban fighting that made the war visible to foreign concessions and foreign cameras. It did not save Nanjing. Nanjing Massacre Nanking Massacre Rape of Nanking After the city fell in December 1937, Japanese troops killed civilians and disarmed soldiers on a mass scale and committed widespread rape. This capsule names the event and does not illustrate it with bodies. Lytton Commission League of Nations commission, 1931–32, led by Lord Lytton, sent to investigate Japan’s seizure of Manchuria after the Mukden Incident. Its report rejected Japan’s account. Japan left the League. The war of 1937 still came. Mukden Incident 18 September 九一八 18 September 1931: an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway used by the Kwantung Army as a pretext to seize Mukden (Shenyang) and then Manchuria. The before of 1937. National Revolutionary Army NRA The Nationalist government’s army, commanded in this war by Chiang Kai-shek. Not the only Chinese armed force in the field; the Communists fought as well, under the United Front’s strained roof. Xi’an Incident December 1936: Zhang Xueliang detained Chiang Kai-shek in Xi’an to force a turn from civil war toward resistance against Japan. The Second United Front follows. A kidnapping as policy. Beiping Peking Beijing The city now called Beijing. In 1937 it was Beiping — “Northern Peace” — because the Nationalist capital was Nanjing. Names in this capsule follow the political geography of the year. Before Manchuria was already a wound On 18 September 1931 the Kwantung Army used an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway as a pretext to seize Mukden and then Manchuria. The League of Nations sent the Lytton Commission. The commissioners walked tracks, took testimony, and produced a report that did not accept Japan’s story. Japan left the League. The occupation stayed. Investigators on a Manchurian railway — the kind of scene the Lytton Commission’s 1931–32 inquiry produced. A League report can name a pretext. It could not put the province back. Men in suits and hats inspecting a railway track in an open landscape. Inside China the 1930s were also a civil war. The Xi’an Incident of December 1936 — Zhang Xueliang detaining Chiang Kai-shek — forced a turn: a Second United Front against Japan. The front was a cease-fire with a shared enemy, not a merger. That is the politics standing behind 7 July 1937. The era From a bridge to a country that had to move On the night of 7 July 1937 a Japanese unit near the Lugou Bridge claimed a missing soldier and demanded entry to Wanping. Shots followed. The incident did not stay local. By the end of the month Beiping and Tianjin were gone. In August the Battle of Shanghai opened a war that foreign concessions could photograph from their own rooftops. Chiang Kai-shek, in the field, looking through binoculars — a wartime command image. The Nationalist state would lose its capital and move the government upriver. The man in the cap is not the whole war. He is the government that had to relocate. Chiang Kai-shek in uniform looking through binoculars, other officers behind him. A civilian pulling a household — chairs, boards, a rocking horse — through a city street. The War of Resistance is a military history. It is also this: millions of people walking inland with what a cart would hold. A man pulling a cart piled with furniture and a child’s rocking horse through a Chinese city street. Nanjing, the capital, fell in December 1937. What followed is the Nanjing Massacre: mass killing of civilians and prisoners, mass rape. This capsule uses one photograph of a city after air attack — rubble, people standing in it, no bodies arranged for the lens. The event does not need a corpse to be believed. If you need numbers, go to the historians who argue over them in public. They are not invented here. A Chinese city after bombing, 1937 — the archive filename places it in Nanjing. People in the frame are standing. This is the one Nanjing image in the capsule: a capital made into a field, not a gallery of the dead. Civilians standing in a wide field of rubble after the bombing of a Chinese city, 1937. The government went to Chongqing. From 1938 the city was bombed, again and again, for years. People lived in tunnels. The wartime capital is not a footnote to the fall of France. It is where the Republic of China was still a state. A Japanese bomber over a river city, smoke on the ground — the archive identifies the campaign against Chongqing. From the air, a capital is a target set. From the ground, it is a schedule of sirens. A Japanese twin-engine bomber over a river city, smoke plumes on the ground. In September 1939 Germany invaded Poland. From London that is when “the war” begins. From Chongqing it is the year the European war joined a war already two years old. The United Front still held, badly. Zhou Enlai in the Nationalist capital was diplomacy as much as alliance. Xiao Hong, who had already fled the Northeast, died in 1942 in Japanese-occupied Hong Kong — a writer’s war, not a general’s. Zhou Enlai (center) with the American journalist Edgar Snow and Deng Yingchao, 1938. The United Front had to be explained to foreigners as well as fought. A photograph of three people standing is not a merger of two parties. Zhou Enlai in a dark suit standing between Edgar Snow and Deng Yingchao. People A general, a diplomat, a writer Chiang Kai-shek 蔣介石 1887–1975 Head of the Nationalist government and commander of the National Revolutionary Army. He lost the coast and kept a state in Sichuan. The after of 1945 is also his. Wartime command photograph. Zhou Enlai 周恩來 1898–1976 Communist representative in the United Front’s public face. Chongqing and the liaison work are part of how the CCP survived the war as a political fact, not only as a guerrilla force. 1938, with Snow and Deng Yingchao. Xiao Hong 蕭紅 1911–1942 Born in the Northeast. The Field of Life and Death and a short life lived as a refugee — Wuhan, Chongqing, Hong Kong. She died in 1942. A war of resistance is also a war of people who were not in uniform. Xiao Hong, a 1930s portrait. A story The rocking horse In the Shanghai refugee photograph the cart is a household turned into a load. The rocking horse is the detail that makes the load a family. This is not a cute war. It is a reminder that “home front” in this war often meant: there is no front that stayed put, and home was something you carried. Europe in 1939 produced its own carts. That does not make 1937 a rehearsal. After 1945, then the war that had been postponed Japan surrendered in August 1945. The United Front did not become a peace. The civil war resumed; by 1949 the People’s Republic was proclaimed in Beijing and the Republic of China’s government was on Taiwan. Memory split with the states. In the PRC the War of Resistance is a founding story. In Taiwan it is also a founding story, with different heroes. In Japan the same years are a different argument still. If a later Friday capsule takes 1945–49, it will not be to tidy this one. It will be because the after is a war of its own. A question Leave this on the table If a world war is dated from 1939, whose 1937 was demoted to a preface? The Battle of China (1944) — Why We Fight U.S. Army orientation film, Frank Capra series. Public-domain American wartime framing of the China theater — useful as a primary object, not as a neutral history. Internet Archive.

subject: literature
title: High modernism (c. 1910–30): the sentence comes apart
dek: Woolf, Joyce, Eliot — and, in the same years, 新青年 and Lu Xun, not as a required Asian peer.
text: High modernism (c. 1910–30): the sentence comes apart Woolf, Joyce, Eliot — and, in the same years, 新青年 and Lu Xun, not as a required Asian peer. c. 1910–30 “High modernism” is a later classroom name for a cluster of European and American experiments with form, especially in the 1910s–20s. The people in this capsule did not agree they were in a school. This capsule looks out from London, Paris, and Dublin — the usual triangle — and then notices that 1918 in Shanghai is the same year, not a sidebar assigned to make the triangle look global. Literature literature 1914 Blast Vorticist magazine, London. Then the war that the type had been rehearsing. 1916 Portrait Joyce’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man appears in book form. 1918 狂人日記 / 新青年 Lu Xun’s “A Madman’s Diary” in New Youth, vol. 4, no. 5. Vernacular Chinese as a literary event. 1919 May Fourth Beijing protests; a political date that literary history also has to hold. 1922 Ulysses / Waste Land Joyce in Paris (Shakespeare and Company); Eliot in London. A year the syllabus never lets go. 1925–27 Woolf Mrs Dalloway; To the Lighthouse. The day, the house, the mind as structure. The Waste Land came with homework When Eliot published The Waste Land in book form in 1922, he added notes. Some explain quotations; some are jokes; some have been treated as a key to a locked poem. He later said the notes began as a way to pad a slim book. Whether you believe the shrug or not, the notes are part of how the poem was sold and taught. A modernist fragment can arrive with its own apparatus. high modernism High modernism modernism Later critical name for early-twentieth-century formal experiment — fragmentation, interiority, mythic scaffolding — especially in English-language literature around 1910–30. The writers did not vote for the label. stream of consciousness A way of writing a mind in motion: associations, sensory fragments, not always a tidy paragraph. Woolf and Joyce are the usual English-language exhibits. The phrase is a critic’s tool, not a 1922 brand name. Ulysses Joyce’s 1922 novel, published in Paris by Shakespeare and Company. One day in Dublin (16 June 1904), a Homeric scaffolding, and a censorship history in the English-speaking world. The Waste Land Waste Land Eliot’s 1922 poem. Fragments, quotations, notes. Ezra Pound cut it. The notes are part of the poem’s public life, not a teacher’s appendix only. Mrs Dalloway Woolf’s 1925 novel. A day in London, a party, a war still in the body of a man who was in it. Time is the structure. Blast Short-lived Vorticist magazine, London, 1914–15, edited by Wyndham Lewis, with Pound among the contributors. Two issues. The cover is a manifesto in type. 新青年 New Youth La Jeunesse Xin Qingnian Chinese magazine, founded 1915 by Chen Duxiu (first as 青年雜誌 / Youth Magazine). The May 1918 issue printed Lu Xun’s “A Madman’s Diary.” It argued for vernacular writing and a new culture in the same years Europe was calling itself modern. May Fourth 五四 May Fourth Movement 4 May 1919: student protests in Beijing against the Versailles settlement’s handling of Shandong. “May Fourth” also names a wider New Culture moment — language, gender, science, the nation — that is not a footnote to London. 狂人日記 A Madman’s Diary Diary of a Madman Lu Xun story, 1918, written in vernacular Chinese. A reader who sees cannibalism in the classical tradition. It is a modernist event in a different language politics. Shakespeare and Company Sylvia Beach’s Paris bookshop. It published Ulysses in 1922 when British and American houses would not. A shop can be a press. Bloomsbury Loose London circle (Woolfs, Bells, Keynes, Strachey, and others). Useful as an address. Fatal as a synonym for all of modernism. Vorticism London avant-garde around Lewis and Blast, briefly, just before and into the First World War. A British answer to Futurism that did not last as a movement and left a very loud magazine. vernacular Chinese 白話 baihua Written Chinese closer to speech, as opposed to classical literary Chinese. The New Culture argument was that literature had to change language, not only subject. Lu Xun’s 1918 story is a landmark in that change. Before A sentence that still believed in sequence The novel and the poem, in the late nineteenth century, could still pretend that time was a corridor. Even when they doubted it, they usually walked you through. The decade before 1914 was already restless — free verse, impressionism, a city speeding up — but the war is the fact that later readers use to explain why the corridor broke. It is not the only fact. Cities, psychoanalysis, new print, and a reading public that included more women and more students were already in the room. Virginia Stephen, photographed by George Charles Beresford in 1902 — years before Mrs Dalloway. The public-domain portrait is of a young woman who had not yet written the books this capsule is about. That is useful. Modernism did not arrive fully formed in a 1922 jacket. Virginia Woolf in profile, 1902, photograph by George Charles Beresford. The era 1922 is a year. 1918 is also a year. From London and Paris the syllabus bunches around 1922: Ulysses from Sylvia Beach’s shop; The Waste Land in The Criterion and then as a book, cut by Pound. Woolf’s major novels come a few years later, but the method is the same family — a day, a mind, a city, a refusal to narrate as if a life were a plot summary. James Joyce, photographed by C. P. Curran in 1918, while Ulysses was still appearing in parts and still unfinished. The book would be a 1922 Paris object. The face is already the one the century kept. Sepia portrait of James Joyce with glasses and a goatee, around 1918. T. S. Eliot, a young man in a study — the usual furniture of the poet as intellectual. The Waste Land (1922) is not a study poem only. It is a collage of other people’s lines, a London of the war’s aftermath, and a set of notes that became part of the work’s public life. T. S. Eliot as a young man in a study, holding a pipe. The same years, not as a required pairing: in Shanghai, 新青年 (New Youth / La Jeunesse) was arguing that Chinese literature had to change its language. The May 1918 issue printed Lu Xun’s 「狂人日記」. In 1919, May Fourth made the argument a street. This is not “the Asian Woolf.” It is a contemporaneous fight about vernacular, the nation, and who a written sentence is for — happening while Eliot was assembling fragments and Joyce was finishing a day in Dublin. 新青年 4:5, May 1918. The contents list includes 魯迅’s 「狂人日記」. The French title La Jeunesse is on the cover. A Shanghai magazine, in the same decade as Blast and Ulysses, announcing that the language of literature would have to change. Cover of New Youth magazine, volume 4 number 5, May 1918, listing 狂人日記 by 魯迅. Lu Xun, Shanghai, 24 September 1930, inscribed at age fifty. The photograph is later than “A Madman’s Diary.” It is the face that the 1918 story, and the years after May Fourth, made public. Studio portrait of Lu Xun in a light changshan, dated Shanghai, 24 September 1930. Blast, in 1914, is the London version of shouting. Two issues, then a war that killed some of the people who might have kept shouting. High modernism is often taught as interior whisper. The pink cover is a reminder that it also wanted to be a poster. People Four writers, one decade, not one school Virginia Woolf 1882–1941 Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927), A Room of One’s Own (1929). The sentence as a record of attention. Bloomsbury is the address, not the whole explanation. Beresford, 1902. James Joyce 1882–1941 Dublin on the page, published in Paris when London and New York were still afraid of the book. Ulysses is a day and a trial and a shop. Curran, 1918. T. S. Eliot 1888–1965 American-born, London-settled. The Waste Land is the poem the century assigned to 1922. The notes, the quotations, and Pound’s cuts are part of the object. A study portrait, early career. Lu Xun 魯迅 1881–1936 Zhou Shuren. “A Madman’s Diary,” then a body of stories, essays, and translations that made vernacular literary Chinese a fact. He is in this capsule because 1918 is 1918 — not because a Western syllabus needed an Asian twin. Shanghai, 1930. A story A magazine cover is also a sentence Blast 1, 1914. The word is the picture. Blast magazine cover, 1914. Put Blast next to 新青年. One is a London roar in English, two issues, a war. The other is a Shanghai magazine that ran for years and printed a story that helped change the written language. They are not the same project. They share a decade in which people decided the old sentence was part of the problem. That is enough of a reason to put them in one capsule. It is not a reason to make one the key to the other. After The syllabus, and what it leaves in the corridor By the 1930s the experiments had become a canon in some places and a target in others. Woolf died in 1941; Joyce the same year; Lu Xun in 1936; Eliot lived to be a monument. The after of high modernism is partly a teaching machine: 1922 as a fetish year, stream of consciousness as a worksheet. The after is also every later writer who inherited the broken corridor and had to decide whether to mend it. If this archive later takes a Thursday to a different literature, it will not be to complete a set. It will be because another year also happened. A question Leave this on the table When a syllabus says “1922,” whose 1918 was dropped to make the year look clean? T. S. Eliot reads The Waste Land (recording) The text is 1922. Recordings circulate legally via libraries and the Poetry Foundation’s page; this is not a film of 1922. James Joyce reads from Finnegans Wake (Anna Livia Plurabelle) Internet Archive copy of Joyce’s own recording. Later than Ulysses; still his voice.

subject: film
title: French New Wave (c. 1958–64): the camera leaves the studio
dek: Truffaut, Godard, Varda as a peer — auteurs, jump cuts, and Paris as a location, not a set.
text: French New Wave (c. 1958–64): the camera leaves the studio Truffaut, Godard, Varda as a peer — auteurs, jump cuts, and Paris as a location, not a set. c. 1958–64 “Nouvelle Vague” was a press label before it was a school. The people in this capsule argued in Cahiers du Cinéma, then made films that did not look like the “tradition of quality” they had been attacking. This capsule looks out from Paris. Japanese New Wave and British Free Cinema are happening in the same years — not assigned Asian or British “peers.” Film film 1954–57 Cahiers Truffaut’s “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français”; the politique des auteurs is a fight about who authors a film. 1955 Varda La Pointe Courte — often called a New Wave film before the name. She is a peer, not a guest. 1959 Cannes Les Quatre Cents Coups. Truffaut the critic becomes Truffaut the director in public. 1960 Breathless À bout de souffle. Jump cuts, handheld, a plot that refuses to behave. 1962 Cléo Cléo de 5 à 7. Two hours in a city, a woman walking, time as a structure. 1960s Elsewhere Japanese New Wave; Free Cinema and the British New Wave. Later cousin, not contemporaneous: Taiwan New Cinema in the 1980s. The jump cuts were also a budget Godard and editor Cécile Decugis shortened Breathless by cutting inside shots, not only between them. The jump cut is now taught as a philosophy of time. It was also a way to lose running time without reshooting Paris. Both things can be true: a device can be an idea and a solution to a reel that was too long. Nouvelle Vague New Wave French New Wave Press name, late 1950s, for a cluster of mostly young French directors who had often been critics first. It is a useful label and a bad census: people were included, excluded, and later added. Cahiers du Cinéma Cahiers French film magazine, founded 1951. Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, Rohmer wrote there. The magazine was a school and a weapon. politique des auteurs auteur auteur theory Cahiers argument: a director can be the author of a film the way a novelist is the author of a book — including in Hollywood, if the films have a signature. In English this hardened into “auteur theory.” It was a polemic, not a law of nature. tradition of quality Tradition of Quality Truffaut’s hostile name for the polished, literary, studio-bound French cinema of the 1940s–50s that Cahiers wanted to replace. “Quality” here is an insult. jump cut jump cuts An edit that skips a bit of time inside a continuous shot, so the image jerks. Breathless made the device famous as style, not as a mistake to be hidden. Cameflex Éclair Cameflex Eclair Cameflex Lightweight French 35mm camera (Éclair). New Wave crews used cameras like this because they could leave the studio. Portability is an aesthetic with a serial number. Left Bank Later grouping of filmmakers including Varda, Resnais, Marker — often more essayistic or Left Bank geographically and temperamentally than the Cahiers men. Useful, and too neat. Free Cinema British mid-1950s documentary movement (Anderson, Reisz, Richardson and others): short films, everyday subjects, a manifesto. It is contemporaneous, not a French export. Japanese New Wave Nuberu Bagu Japanese 1960s directors (Oshima, Imamura, Teshigahara and others) breaking with studio form. The name borrows the French phrase. The films do not. New Hollywood U.S. late-1960s/1970s studio crash and youth-market turn. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the usual bridge sentence from the New Wave. A later effect, not a twin. Taiwan New Cinema 1980s Taiwanese film movement (Hou Hsiao-hsien, Edward Yang, and others). A later cousin in the family of “new cinemas,” not a 1960 contemporary. Cannes The festival that, in 1959, made Les Quatre Cents Coups an international event. A prize is not a movement, but it is how a movement gets a date. Before Critics with a grudge, and a camera that could walk In the 1950s a set of Paris critics used Cahiers du Cinéma to pick a fight with their own national cinema. Truffaut’s 1954 essay “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” attacked what he called the tradition of quality: well-upholstered literary adaptations, studio craft, a cinema that looked finished and felt, to him, dead. The politique des auteurs was the other half of the fight. A director, even in Hollywood, could be an author. Hitchcock counted. So did Hawks. The insult to the French studio system was the point. An Éclair Cameflex, the kind of relatively light 35mm camera Paris rental houses such as Chevereau supplied. New Wave form is often taught as an idea. It is also a kit that could be carried into a street. An Éclair Cameflex 35mm movie camera on a tripod, labeled Eclair Paris and Chevereau. They were not the first people to want a camera outside. Italian neorealism had already taken the war’s rubble as a set. What was new in Paris was the combination: critics who became directors, a magazine that had already trained an audience, and equipment that made a low budget look like a choice. The era 1959 is a date. It is not the whole map. Les Quatre Cents Coups premiered at Cannes in 1959. Truffaut, who had been banned from the festival as a critic, arrived as a director. The film follows Antoine Doinel through a Paris that is not a postcard — school, streets, a runaway, a freeze-frame on a beach. It is the date the press needed. It is not the first film in the cluster. The Latin Quarter as a working street, not a back lot. New Wave location shooting made Paris look like a place people already lived — which is why the city in these films still feels like itself, and why a production still needed permits, light, and luck. Paris street toward the Panthéon, late 1950s. À bout de souffle (1960) is the film people mean when they say “jump cut.” Godard and his editor cut inside shots; time skips; the hero talks to the camera as if the fourth wall were optional. The plot is a thin crime story. The event is the grammar. Agnès Varda is not a cameo in a men’s movement. La Pointe Courte (1955) is often called a New Wave film before the name existed. Cléo de 5 à 7 (1962) walks a singer through two real-time hours of Paris while she waits for a medical result. If “auteur” only fits the Cahiers men, the word is too small — the same problem a later feminism lesson will have with “first wave.” Agnès Varda (left), early 1960s. The filename on this archive print says Venice, 1962 — the year of Cléo. Treat the place-name as the archive’s label. The person is not in doubt: a director who was already working when the magazine men picked up cameras. Agnès Varda, short dark hair, standing with another woman on a wooden deck over water. A later photograph of a portable camera on a tripod, children looking through the finder. This is not a 1959 production still. It is here because the New Wave’s bet — that a lighter camera changes who gets to shoot, and where — did not stay in Paris. The kit traveled. The date of this picture is later than the era. The idea is the era’s. Children looking through a professional motion-picture camera on a tripod, with an adult nearby. The same years, elsewhere: in Japan, Oshima, Imamura, Teshigahara and others were breaking studio form; the Japanese phrase nūberu bāgu borrows the French name and then goes its own way. In Britain, Free Cinema’s shorts and manifesto (Anderson, Reisz, Richardson) had already argued for everyday subjects and a camera that did not owe the studio a polished lie. These are contemporaneous arguments, not a seating chart with France at the head. People Three directors, not a trinity François Truffaut 1932–1984 Critic, then director. Les Quatre Cents Coups made the movement a Cannes story. He kept coming back to Antoine Doinel. The man who attacked the tradition of quality became, in time, a tradition of his own — which is a later capsule. Jean-Luc Godard 1930–2022 À bout de souffle, then a career of breaking the toy he had just been given. Jump cuts are the textbook; the longer fact is a director who treated cinema as an argument that could be continued in public. Agnès Varda 1928–2019 Photographer first, then filmmaker. La Pointe Courte, Cléo, and decades of work after the New Wave name had gone cold. If a syllabus puts her in a sidebar, the syllabus is the artifact. A peer, not a supporting role. A story Who gets to be the author The politique des auteurs was a way of watching Hollywood with respect and watching French “quality” with contempt. It gave critics a hero: the director as signature. It also made it easy to miss the editor, the cinematographer, the producer, the actor who is carrying the film. Breathless without Raoul Coutard’s camera, or without Jean Seberg’s face, is a different object. Varda’s career is a useful correction: the author can be a woman who was never on the Cahiers masthead as a boy critic. Keep the Cameflex in mind. Authorship, in this era, is also a question of who can afford to leave the studio, and who is allowed to. After New Hollywood, and a cousin who arrives late American studios in the late 1960s needed a younger audience and had lost the old Production Code’s certainty. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the sentence film histories use to connect Paris to New Hollywood. The connection is real and incomplete. A lot of other things — television, the draft, the collapse of the studio system’s weekly habit — were in that room. Taiwan New Cinema, in the 1980s, is sometimes filed as another “new wave.” It is a later cousin: a different state, a different language politics, a different argument with its own studios. It does not belong on the 1958–64 timeline except as a reminder that the French name traveled, and that travel is not the same as origin. A question Leave this on the table If the director is the author, whose names have to wait in the credits? The 400 Blows — Criterion film page Legal home-video edition. This capsule does not link a pirated full film. Breathless — Criterion film page À bout de souffle, 1960. Again: the licensed edition, not a rip. Cléo from 5 to 7 — Criterion film page Varda, 1962. Watch a legal copy. BFI — Free Cinema Britain, same years: a manifesto and a set of shorts, not a French franchise.

subject: music
title: British Invasion (c. 1963–67): selling America its own records back
dek: From skiffle and pirate ships to Beatles, Stones, and Kinks — and the Black American records they had been learning from.
text: British Invasion (c. 1963–67): selling America its own records back From skiffle and pirate ships to Beatles, Stones, and Kinks — and the Black American records they had been learning from. c. 1963–67 “British Invasion” is an American radio and press name for British beat groups hitting the U.S. charts after 1964. From London the same years were also pirate radio, a BBC that still rationed pop, and a generation that had learned guitar from American R&B records. This capsule looks out from Britain. It does not treat Motown or Tokyo as decoration. Music music 1956 Skiffle Lonnie Donegan’s “Rock Island Line” makes a U.S. folk-blues song a British teenage instrument kit. 1962 Liverpool / London Beatles sign to Parlophone; the London R&B clubs are already covering Chess and Motown. 1964 Ed Sullivan / Caroline Beatles on U.S. television in February; Radio Caroline begins offshore in March. 1964 Kinks / Stones “You Really Got Me”; the Stones keep the Chicago debt louder than the suits would like. 1965–66 Elsewhere Motown and Stax in the U.S.; Group Sounds in Japan; yé-yé already on French radio. 1967 Door ajar Sgt. Pepper and the turn toward psychedelia. The Invasion name starts to look too small. The BBC had a needle-time problem Into the mid-1960s the BBC was bound by “needle time”: agreements with the Musicians’ Union that limited how many hours of records (as opposed to live studio bands) could be broadcast. Pirate ships were not just teenage romance. They were a way around a labor and licensing rule. Radio 1, created in 1967, was in part an official answer to that gap. British Invasion American press and radio name, from 1964, for the rush of British beat groups onto the U.S. charts. The people in Liverpool and London did not need the phrase to know they were already playing. skiffle British 1950s homemade jazz-folk-blues: acoustic guitar, washboard, tea-chest bass. Lonnie Donegan’s hit version of “Rock Island Line” (1955–56) put a cheap guitar in a lot of teenage hands, including future Beatles and Stones. R&B rhythm and blues In early-1960s Britain, “R&B” usually meant Black American rhythm and blues and Chicago electric blues — Chess Records, Motown, the records imported or covered in London clubs — not the later pop-chart sense of the letters. pirate radio Radio Caroline Unlicensed stations on ships or forts outside British territorial waters, from 1964. They played the records the BBC’s Light Programme would not schedule in bulk. Radio Caroline began in March 1964. Chess Chess Records Chicago label (Phil and Leonard Chess) that recorded Chuck Berry, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf. British groups learned the catalog; American radio had often filed it as “race” or R&B, not pop. Motown Detroit label founded by Berry Gordy. By 1964 it was a hit factory with its own sound, choreography, and crossover ambition — running in the same years as the Invasion, not waiting to be discovered by it. Stax Memphis label (and studio) whose house band and singers made Southern soul in the mid-1960s. Otis Redding, Booker T. & the M.G.’s, later Isaac Hayes. Another American industry, contemporaneous, not a British invention. Group Sounds グループ・サウンズ Japanese 1960s electric-guitar pop, mid-decade: The Tigers, The Spiders, The Blue Comets. It heard the Beatles and local kayōkyoku at once. Same years, different market. yé-yé French (and wider European) mid-1960s pop named for the “yeah-yeah” refrain. France Gall, Sylvie Vartan, and others were already on the radio while Britain was invading America. Vox AC30 AC30 British 30-watt guitar amplifier, from the late 1950s. The Beatles, the Shadows, and later the Invasion groups used it. The chime is a hardware fact, not a metaphor. Ed Sullivan Sunday-night U.S. television variety show. The Beatles’ 9 February 1964 appearance is the Invasion’s most repeated American date. It was a broadcast, not the beginning of the music. Parlophone EMI label that signed the Beatles in 1962, with George Martin as producer. Not a small indie — a wing of a large British record company that had room for comedy records and, it turned out, beat groups. Before A guitar, a washboard, and other people’s records Postwar Britain had American records before it had a name for what to do with them. Rhythm and blues and rock and roll arrived as classified imports, as merchant-seamen singles, as the B-sides of things the Light Programme did not love. Chuck Berry’s “Johnny B. Goode” was a 1958 Chess single from Chicago. In Britain it was homework. Chuck Berry, late-1950s publicity photograph. British beat groups did not invent this stance. They learned it from records and from the few U.S. package tours that reached them. Chuck Berry in a tuxedo, crouched, playing a Gibson electric guitar. Chess 1691, “Johnny B. Goode,” 1958. The label is the object: Chicago, two and a half minutes, C. Berry. A decade later British groups were still arguing about who owned the riff. Blue Chess Records 45 label for Johnny B. Goode by Chuck Berry, catalog 1691. Skiffle made the homework cheap. Lonnie Donegan’s “Rock Island Line” — a Lead Belly song, recorded in London — became a British hit in 1956. A washboard and a tea-chest bass were enough to start a group. John Lennon’s Quarrymen were a skiffle band. So were half the people who later grew fringes. The BBC did not refuse pop. It rationed it. Needle-time agreements limited recorded music on air. If you wanted more than the official dose, you needed a radio that was not polite, or a ship that was not in British waters yet. The era Britain looks at America, and America looks back From London and Liverpool the story is not “we invented rock.” It is: we learned these records, we played them faster and louder in rooms the size of a pub, and then American television decided we were a phenomenon. The Beatles’ “I Want to Hold Your Hand” reached the U.S. in late 1963. On 9 February 1964 they played The Ed Sullivan Show. The phrase “British Invasion” is what American radio called the months that followed. A mid-1960s transistor radio. The Invasion needed ships and television, but it also needed a private speaker a teenager could hold. The BBC was a household set. This was a pocket. Black portable Orion eight-transistor radio with a gold speaker grille. The Rolling Stones kept the Chicago debt in the foreground: Chess covers, a longer haircut, a refusal to be variety. The Kinks, in 1964, put a sliced speaker cone under “You Really Got Me” and made a London riff that did not sound like a cover. None of this erases Berry, or Motown, or the fact that American pop radio had often kept those sources in a separate chart. MV Caroline, the first Radio Caroline ship. The station began broadcasting in March 1964 from international waters. It was a business and a workaround: records the BBC would not play in bulk, aimed at the same teenagers who were about to watch Sullivan. The ship Caroline at sea, name painted on the bow, masts and a dark funnel against a pale sky. The same years, not as a required pair: in Detroit, Motown was already a finished system — writers, a house band, a finishing school for movement. In Memphis, Stax was cutting Southern soul with a biracial house band. In Japan, Group Sounds bands were taking electric guitars into a market that had its own kayōkyoku tradition. In France, yé-yé was already a word. Britain was not the only place the 45 rpm single was rewriting a generation. It was the place American television decided to point the camera. A Vox AC30 Twin, the British amp on a lot of Invasion stages. The tag in this photograph guesses at a Shadows connection. Treat the guess as a guess. The hardware is the fact: 30 watts, two speakers, a sound that is not a Fender. A worn Vox AC30 Twin guitar amplifier with diamond grille cloth and a handwritten museum tag. People Who is in the room when the records change hands Chuck Berry 1926–2017 St. Louis guitarist, Chess Records. British groups covered him so often the covers became a curriculum. The Invasion’s joke — selling America its own Black music back — is a joke with his name on the label. The source, not the opening act. Lonnie Donegan 1931–2002 Scottish-born skiffle singer. “Rock Island Line” (1955–56) showed a British teenager that an American folk-blues song could be a hit without an orchestra. The washboard years are the unglamorous before. The Beatles 1960–1970 as a group Liverpool, then Hamburg, then Parlophone. This capsule does not need another press shot of four men in suits. The relevant fact is the repertoire: Berry, Little Richard, girl-group records, and then songs of their own that American radio could not file as “foreign novelty” for long. Berry Gordy b. 1929 Founder of Motown. In 1964 his label was not waiting to be invaded. It was already teaching America a different lesson about who got to be pop. A story The same riff, two charts Put the Chess label next to a 1964 British 45. The guitar figure is often cousin to cousin. The difference is the filing cabinet. American pop radio had spent the 1950s learning how to separate “race records” from the hit parade, then how to let a few of them through. British teenagers, a few years later, heard the same Chess and Motown singles as the whole of modern music. When they sent the sound back, it arrived as white faces on Sullivan. That is not a small fact. It is the fact. The honest version does not scold the British groups for learning. It asks who got paid, who got booked, and which name the camera learned first. After Psychedelia, and the name that stopped fitting By 1966–67 the useful Invasion story — verse, chorus, suit, scream — was already too small. Revolver, then Sgt. Pepper, then a lot of other people’s sitars and tape loops. The door toward psychedelia is not a British monopoly either; San Francisco and Lagos and Lagos’s records in London are all in the same late decade. The name “British Invasion” stays useful as a 1964–65 American chart event. It is a poor name for everything that happened next. Radio 1 began in 1967. The pirates were legislated against. The records did not go back in the box. A question Leave this on the table If a country sells another country its own music, who is the inventor in the room? The Beatles on The Ed Sullivan Show (9 February 1964) Sullivan’s own site on the broadcast. Full performances are licensed; this is the historical record of the date, not a bootleg film. Chuck Berry — Johnny B. Goode (1958) Chess single 1691. The record many British groups learned from. Official/label upload; if it moves, search the title on the label’s channel. The Beatles — I Want to Hold Your Hand (1963) The Capitol single that opened the U.S. door in late 1963 / early 1964. Official Beatles channel. The Kinks — You Really Got Me (1964) Official audio. Distorted riff, London, not Liverpool. The Temptations — My Girl (1964) Motown, same year as the Sullivan appearance. Not a footnote — a parallel industry. Radio Caroline The station still exists. The 1964 ship is history; the site is the living remnant, not a 1964 tape.

subject: feminism
title: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): who got to count as a “woman” in public
dek: Suffrage, splits, and the people the word “we” left out.
text: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): who got to count as a “woman” in public Suffrage, splits, and the people the word “we” left out. c. 1848–1920 “First wave” is a later Anglo-American label, not a name the people in this capsule used for themselves. It is useful as a frame — a span of public fights over whether women counted as political persons — and incomplete as a history. What follows uses the frame, then looks at the same decades elsewhere. A story The shadow and the substance Sojourner Truth, 1864. She sold the card because lectures did not pay enough. She also put her own copyright on it. Sojourner Truth’s 1864 carte-de-visite, with the printed line I sell the shadow to support the substance under her portrait. Truth sold her image because lectures did not pay enough. The “shadow” is the photograph — a thing that can be reproduced, captioned, passed from hand to hand. The “substance” is the work, and the body that had been treated as property. She put the sentence on the card in English, under her own name, and made the sale part of the argument: I will be paid for the copy of me that you can hold. Keep the card in mind when a movement talks about “women” as if the category were already settled. Someone is always deciding which body is the subject, and which body is the illustration. After The vote, the doldrums, and the staircase In the United States the 1920s through the 1950s are often called the “doldrums”: the vote arrived, the coalition thinned. The word is a weather report written after the fact. It describes a particular organized feminism going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended. What gets called the second wave — the 1960s and 1970s — turned to the workplace, to sexuality, to housework. “The personal is political.” The who-counts problem returned in public, including in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977, which refused to treat race, sex, and class as separate queues. The wave metaphor itself is the after. It offers a tidy staircase: first the vote, then the rest. It hides the people who were never on the stairs — and the fights that did not wait for the next numbered swell.
